Madeira lanternfish (Ceratoscopelus maderensis) is a mesopelagic myctophid widely distributed across the eastern North Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. Individuals in this population attain a maximum standard length of 8.9 centimeters [Li = 8.9 centimeters], which is comparable to values reported for other vertically migrating myctophids from temperate waters. Field surveys conducted using midwater trawls indicate that adults typically range between 6 and 8 centimeters, with the upper end of the size distribution rarely exceeding this asymptotic value. Growth increments, inferred from otolith microstructural analysis, suggest that this ultimate length is reached after a prolonged juvenile period characterized by relatively slow somatic expansion. This species exhibits a moderate degree of sexual dimorphism in body size, with females tending to be slightly larger than males across most sampled populations. Regional variation in temperature and prey availability may further modulate maximum attainable size, as specimens collected from warmer southerly latitudes often present slightly smaller asymptotic lengths compared to their conspecifics from cooler northern sectors of the species range.

Reproductive development in Ceratoscopelus maderensis follows a pattern typical of many small mesopelagic teleosts. Puberty is attained once individuals reach a standard length of 5 centimeters [Lp = 5 centimeters], a size threshold that corresponds to roughly fifty-six percent of the ultimate adult length. Histological examination of gonadal tissue reveals that vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis commence around this size, marking the transition from the immature juvenile stage to a reproductively capable adult. The wet weight at this developmental milestone is approximately 0.81 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.81 grams], a modest body mass that reflects the relatively compressed growth trajectory of this species during its first year of life. The allometric relationship between length and mass in this species follows a power function similar to that described for other myctophids, with the exponent indicating slightly positive allometric growth. This implies that as the fish increase in length, their body mass increases at a proportionally greater rate, which may facilitate the accumulation of energy reserves necessary for successful spawning.

Maximum reproductive output in Madeira lanternfish has been investigated under controlled laboratory conditions simulating the thermal regime of their natural habitat at a stable water temperature of 8.6 °C [T = 8.6 °C]. Under these conditions, females exhibit a maximum reproductive rate of approximately 26 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 26 eggs per day], which is sustained over the course of a protracted spawning season. This figure is derived from the observation that gravid females produce roughly 9,632 eggs over a 365 day period, yielding an estimated maximum reproductive rate of about 26.4 eggs per day [Ri = about 26.4 eggs per day]. The pelagic eggs are small and transparent, measuring approximately 1 millimeter in diameter, and the wet weight at birth for a newly hatched larva is calculated at 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], based on the egg volume. This minimal birth mass is typical of myctophid larvae, which rely on endogenous yolk reserves for the first several days following eclosion before transitioning to exogenous feeding on small copepod nauplii.

Adult body mass in Ceratoscopelus maderensis reaches an ultimate wet weight of approximately 5 grams [Wwi = approximately 5 grams] for fully grown individuals, a value derived from empirical length-mass regressions based on extensive sampling across the species geographic range. This asymptotic mass is attained concurrently with the maximum standard length, indicating that somatic growth essentially plateaus once the fish reach their ultimate size. The relationship between length and mass follows a curvilinear pattern typical of fusiform teleosts, with larger individuals exhibiting a disproportionate increase in body mass relative to length. This allometric scaling likely reflects the accumulation of gonadal tissue and lipid reserves in preparation for seasonal spawning events. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this ultimate wet weight is consistent with that of other medium-sized myctophids occupying similar trophic niches in the mesopelagic zone, though local environmental conditions can introduce modest variation around this mean value.

Lifespan estimates for Madeira lanternfish indicate a maximum longevity of approximately 803 days [am = approximately 803 days] when maintained at a constant temperature of 8.6 °C [T = 8.6 °C], which corresponds to about 2.2 years. This relatively short lifespan is characteristic of many small myctophids inhabiting warm-temperate and subtropical waters, where elevated metabolic rates and high predation pressure from piscivorous fishes and cephalopods drive rapid population turnover. Age determination using otolith sagittae reveals that the majority of individuals complete their life cycle within two years, with very few specimens surviving beyond this age in natural populations. The species exhibits a semelparous-like reproductive strategy in which a single prolonged spawning season occupies much of the second year of life, followed by a steep increase in natural mortality as energy reserves become depleted. This life history pattern aligns well with the fast-paced demographic strategy typical of small pelagic forage fishes.
